question: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In recent months, there has been a noticeable trend in which an increasing number of influencers are reporting on their accounts that their content on Instagram is being restricted, their reach reduced or their accounts suspended. The majority of these influencers call out hate speech, share information about sex, women’s health1 and self-determination, or are part of the LGBTQI community2 – such as @sammlungderschande, @klartext_mit_lilly, @womenhelporg in Poland, @stopcryingjosiie and @marieejoan3. They report that their accounts have been subject to reach restrictions or suspended without transparent or reasonable justifications. This situation raises fundamental questions about freedom of expression in the EU. When large, mostly non-European platforms decide what content sees the light of day, it makes it seem that external actors have a significant influence on public discourse in Europe. This affects not only individual users, but democratic debate culture as a whole. Against this background, the question arises as to whether Meta is sufficiently complying with its obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA), in particular as regards the obligation to provide clear and specific statements of reasons (Article 17), functioning and accessible internal complaint procedures (Article 20) and risk assessment (Article 34). Does the Commission intend to launch formal procedures to assess whether Meta is in breach of these DSA provisions?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the issue referred to and is in touch with relevant stakeholders. Under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, providers of very large online platforms (such as Facebook and Instagram) and of very large online search engines, are required to diligently identify, analyse and assess systemic risks stemming from their services and to put in place effective measures to mitigate the identified risks. This includes risks of any actual or foreseeable negative effects for the exercise of fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and of information, including media pluralism, and on electoral processes and civic discourse. In 2024, the Commission initiated proceedings under the DSA against Meta, including in relation to its suspicion that the recommender systems of Facebook and Instagram demote political content and that Meta had failed to put in place an effective internal complainthandling system2. On 24 October 2025, the Commission preliminarily found Meta, inter alia, in breach of its obligation to put in place an effective internal complaint-handling system3. The Commission is not in a position to comment on the details of its investigation, beyond publicly available information. The Commission is continuously monitoring Meta’s compliance with the DSA, engages in regulatory dialogue, and has sent requests for information, including on Meta’s obligations under the DSA regarding the assessment and mitigation of systemic risks, the provision of clear and specific statements of reason, and transparency obligations4. It is Meta’s responsibility to comply with all applicable EU and national laws, including the DSA and other provisions protecting freedom of expression.
